mcq.prompt: How does `flags & snapshot == 0` actually group?
choices: flags & (snapshot == 0)
(flags & snapshot) == (0)
It is ill-formed without parentheses
(flags & snapshot) == 0
mcq.explain: Equality binds more tightly than bitwise AND. The comparison yields false, which converts to 0, and `flags & 0` is always 0 — so the test is a constant false regardless of the flags. Always parenthesise the mask: (flags & snapshot) == 0.

mcq.prompt: How does `1 << level + 1` group?
choices: (1 << level) + 1
1 << (level + 1)
1 << level, then + 1 is discarded
It is ambiguous
mcq.explain: Addition binds more tightly than shift, so this is 1 << (level + 1) — twice what a reader skimming for `1 << level` expects. The rule to take away is not the precedence table but the habit: parenthesise whenever the grouping required thought.

mcq.prompt: What is the type of `use_model ? ticks : model_price` where ticks is int and model_price is double?
choices: The expression is ill-formed — the operands differ in type
int
double
It depends on the runtime value of use_model
mcq.explain: The conditional operator produces one result type determined at compile time from both alternatives, using the usual arithmetic conversions. ticks converts to double, so the type is double whichever branch is taken.

mcq.prompt: How does `quantity += fill` differ from `quantity = quantity + fill`?
choices: It suppresses integer promotion of the operands
There is no difference at all
It is faster because it compiles to a single instruction
The left operand is evaluated only once
mcq.explain: Compound assignment evaluates its left operand once. That is invisible for a plain variable but matters when the left side is `buckets[index()]` or contains any other call — the naive expansion would run it twice.

mcq.prompt: Which pair of properties defines an xvalue?
choices: Has identity, expiring
No identity, not expiring
Has identity, not expiring
No identity, expiring
mcq.explain: An xvalue has identity and is marked as expiring — std::move(x) is the canonical example. An lvalue has identity and is not expiring; a prvalue has no identity and is treated as expiring. glvalue and rvalue are the two umbrella categories over these three.

mcq.prompt: A variable is declared `int&& r = 7;`. What is the value category of the expression `r`?
choices: xvalue
lvalue
It depends on how r is used
prvalue
mcq.explain: A named variable is an lvalue even when its type is an rvalue reference. Classify the *expression*, not the declared type — this is exactly why std::move exists, to turn the lvalue expression r back into an xvalue.

mcq.prompt: Why does `int& bad = quantity + 1;` fail to compile?
choices: References must be initialised with a named variable
The addition might overflow
quantity + 1 is a prvalue, and a non-const lvalue reference cannot bind to it
quantity + 1 has the wrong type
mcq.explain: Only const T& (or T&&) may bind to a prvalue. `const int& read_only = quantity + 1;` compiles and extends the temporary's lifetime. The same rule explains why an assignment target must be a modifiable lvalue: (quantity + 1) = 7 is ill-formed.

mcq.prompt: In C++17 and later, what is the status of `consume(i++, i++)`?
choices: Well-defined — arguments always evaluate left to right
Ill-formed — the compiler must reject it
Undefined behaviour — two unsequenced modifications of i
Unspecified — the two increments are indeterminately sequenced, so the result depends on which runs first
mcq.explain: C++17 made function arguments indeterminately sequenced: each argument completes before the next begins, but the order is the implementation's choice. Before C++17 they were unsequenced and this was undefined behaviour. Unspecified is better than undefined, but it still must not carry program logic.

mcq.prompt: Which of these is undefined behaviour in C++17?
choices: consume(first(), second());
mcq.explain: `i = i++ + i++` contains two unsequenced modifications of the same scalar — still undefined. `i = i++ + 1` became well-defined in C++17 because the whole right operand of assignment is sequenced before the left, and `a[i] = i++` is likewise ordered by the C++17 rule that the right operand of = comes first.

mcq.prompt: `publish(next_bid(), next_ask());` where both helpers increment a shared counter. What is the defect?
choices: It is undefined behaviour in C++17
Which argument receives the value 1 is unspecified
The two calls may interleave with each other
Nothing — arguments evaluate left to right
mcq.explain: The calls do not interleave (C++17 forbids that), and nothing here is undefined. But the order is the implementation's choice, so the sequence numbers may land in either parameter. Compute the side effects in separate statements when the order carries meaning.

mcq.prompt: Which category must the implementation document its choice for?
choices: Undefined behaviour
Unspecified behaviour
Implementation-defined behaviour
All three
mcq.explain: Implementation-defined behaviour — the signedness of plain char, the size of long — requires the implementation to pick a permitted choice and document it, so code may rely on it under an explicit platform contract. Unspecified behaviour is chosen per occurrence with no announcement; undefined behaviour has no requirements at all.

mcq.prompt: `bool wraps(int value) { return value + 1 < value; }` compiles to `xor eax, eax; ret` — an unconditional false. Why is that legal?
choices: It is a compiler bug that -O0 would avoid
The comparison is unspecified, so any answer is permitted
The compiler proved that int addition saturates rather than wraps
For every input on which the addition is defined, value + 1 > value; the overflow case has undefined behaviour, so the optimiser need not preserve it
mcq.explain: The optimiser may assume undefined behaviour never occurs on a path a valid program takes. Calling wraps(INT_MAX) does not make it return true — the call simply has undefined behaviour. The language contract, not the hardware's wraparound, is what the compiler is required to honour.

mcq.prompt: A build runs clean under UBSan and ASan. What may you conclude?
choices: The program contains no undefined behaviour on the paths that were executed, for the checks those sanitizers instrument
The program contains no undefined behaviour in the translation units that were instrumented
Nothing — sanitizers produce too many false negatives to be evidence
The program contains no undefined behaviour
mcq.explain: Sanitizers detect only the cases they instrument, and only on executed paths. Uninitialised reads need MemorySanitizer, data races need ThreadSanitizer. A clean run is evidence, not proof.

mcq.prompt: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
choices: A parameter is passed by value; an argument by reference
A parameter is the local name in the declaration; an argument is the expression supplied by a call
They are interchangeable terms
A parameter belongs to a member function; an argument to a free function
mcq.explain: The parameter is the declaration-side name, the argument is the call-side expression. The distinction matters when discussing conversions: it is the argument that is converted to the parameter's type, and the ranking of that conversion is what overload resolution compares.

mcq.prompt: `auto spread(double bid, double ask) -> double` differs from `double spread(double bid, double ask)` how?
choices: The trailing form deduces the return type at instantiation
The trailing form is a declaration only and needs a separate definition
They mean the same thing
The trailing form disables copy elision on return
mcq.explain: The trailing-return spelling is purely syntactic here. It earns its keep when the return type must mention the parameters — e.g. `auto f(T a, U b) -> decltype(a + b)` — which is not possible with the leading form.

mcq.prompt: Unqualified lookup finds a name in an inner scope. What happens to declarations of the same name in enclosing scopes?
choices: They participate only if the inner declaration is not viable
The program is ill-formed due to ambiguity
They are merged into one overload set
They are hidden — lookup stops at the first scope containing the name
mcq.explain: Unqualified lookup works outward and stops at the first scope containing the name; outer declarations are hidden, not combined. This is why a local `int timeout` completely shadows a namespace-scope `timeout`, and why an inner member function hides base-class overloads of the same name.

mcq.prompt: Why should `using namespace std;` never appear in a header?
choices: Every source file that includes the header inherits the exposed names and their collisions
It is ill-formed at namespace scope
It prevents argument-dependent lookup from working
It slows compilation measurably
mcq.explain: A using-directive in a header is inflicted on every translation unit that includes it, transitively, with no way for those files to opt out. A using-*declaration* inside a function body (`using std::cout;`) is scoped and harmless.

mcq.prompt: Given overloads pick(int), pick(long) and pick(double), which does `pick(small)` select for a `short small`?
choices: The call is ambiguous
pick(int)
pick(long)
pick(double)
mcq.explain: short to int is an integer promotion, which outranks the integral and floating conversions needed for the other two candidates. Overload resolution compares conversion ranks — it does not reason about which destination type is 'closest' in width.

mcq.prompt: Given the same three overloads, what happens for `unsigned quantity = 42; pick(quantity);`?
choices: pick(int) wins — same width
pick(long) wins — long can represent every unsigned int value
The call is ambiguous — all three candidates need a conversion-rank conversion
pick(double) wins — floating conversions outrank integral ones
mcq.explain: unsigned int to int, to long, and to double are all ranked simply as 'conversion'. No candidate is better than the others for the only argument, so there is no unique best viable function and compilation fails. Overload sets split across signed and unsigned integers are a reliable source of this.

mcq.prompt: Given `void inspect(int&)` and `void inspect(const int&)`, which is selected by `inspect(3)`?
choices: Ambiguous
Ill-formed — a literal cannot bind to any reference
inspect(int&)
inspect(const int&)
mcq.explain: 3 is a prvalue and cannot bind to a non-const lvalue reference, so only const int& is viable. For a modifiable lvalue like `int live`, the int& overload wins because it avoids the added const qualification.

mcq.prompt: Why does `std::cout << order` find an operator<< defined as a friend inside `trading::Order`?
choices: Because argument-dependent lookup searches namespaces and classes associated with the argument types
Because std::ostream declares a template that matches any type
Because operator overloads bypass name lookup entirely
Because friends are injected into the enclosing namespace by ordinary lookup
mcq.explain: Operator notation is an unqualified call, and ADL adds the namespaces and classes associated with the arguments — here both std and trading. A hidden friend is invisible to ordinary namespace lookup and findable only this way, which keeps it out of unrelated candidate sets.

mcq.prompt: Why is `using std::swap; swap(left, right);` preferred over `std::swap(left, right);`?
choices: std::swap is deprecated in C++23
The unqualified call lets ADL find a type-specific swap, with std::swap as the fallback
The qualified call cannot bind to references
It avoids one function call at runtime
mcq.explain: This is the two-step idiom. The using-declaration puts std::swap in the candidate set; the unqualified call lets ADL add trading::swap, which is a better match for trading::Quote. Calling std::swap directly suppresses that customisation point entirely.

mcq.prompt: `void publish(std::string symbol = load_primary_symbol());` — when does load_primary_symbol() run?
choices: Once, when the declaration is first seen
Once, the first time publish() is called with no argument
At every call that omits the argument
Never — the default is evaluated lazily inside the function
mcq.explain: A default argument is an expression evaluated at each call that omits it. A costly default is therefore a cost the call site cannot see: `publish();` builds a std::string and calls a function that is nowhere in that line of source.

mcq.prompt: `auto f(bool b) { if (b) return 1; return 1.0; }` — what happens?
choices: It compiles but the return type is unspecified
It compiles; the return type is double, and 1 converts
It compiles; the return type is int, and 1.0 truncates
It is ill-formed — deduced return expressions must agree exactly
mcq.explain: Every non-discarded return expression must deduce the same type; the compiler does not look for a common arithmetic type the way the conditional operator does. Related rule: a recursive call is only valid after an earlier return has established the type.

mcq.prompt: What do [[likely]] and [[unlikely]] do?
choices: Hint block layout and fall-through choices to the compiler
Insert hardware branch-prediction hints into the instruction stream
Force the compiler to remove the unlikely branch
Make a branch condition more probable at runtime
mcq.explain: They influence code layout — which block falls through, which is placed out of line. They cannot change how often a condition is true, and a wrong hint can worsen instruction fetch. Measure before adding them.

mcq.prompt: Why must you write `(order_pointer->*notional_member)()` rather than `order_pointer->*notional_member()`?
choices: Because member-function pointers must always be parenthesised
Because the function-call operator binds more tightly than ->*, so the unparenthesised form tries to call the pointer before applying it to the object
Because ->* returns a reference that must be materialised first
Because the const qualifier on the member function requires it
mcq.explain: The member-pointer operators .* and ->* have lower precedence than a function call, so the unparenthesised spelling parses as `order_pointer->*(notional_member())` and does not compile. This is one place where the parentheses are not stylistic.

mcq.prompt: What problem does std::invoke solve?
choices: It allows a member function to be called without an object
It makes indirect calls faster by devirtualising them
It gives one call syntax to free functions, function pointers, member pointers and function objects
It owns the callable, unlike a raw function pointer
mcq.explain: Direct calls need four different spellings — fp(a, b), order.*pm, (order.*pmf)(), fn(x). std::invoke(callable, args...) covers them all, which is what makes generic adapters writable. Owning the callable is std::function's job, not invoke's.

mcq.prompt: `std::printf("%d\n", 3.14);` — what is the status of this call?
choices: It is well-defined; printf converts the double to int
It is ill-formed and will not compile
It prints a garbage integer, which is implementation-defined
It is undefined behaviour: %d promises int, the argument is a double
mcq.explain: Variadic arguments undergo default promotions and the callee retrieves exactly the type the format promised. Retrieving an int where a double was passed is undefined behaviour. -Wformat diagnoses it for a literal format string; a format assembled at runtime defeats that check entirely.

mcq.prompt: On the SysV x86-64 ABI, what happens to `double sum(Order order)` where Order holds two doubles?
choices: Both fields can arrive in xmm registers, so the callee needs no memory access
The struct is always passed through an invisible pointer
The call is rejected — aggregates cannot be passed by value
The Order is copied to the stack and its address passed in rdi
mcq.explain: A 16-byte trivially copyable aggregate of two doubles satisfies the ABI classification for register passing: the body can be a single addsd. The const Order& version instead passes an address in rdi and issues two dependent loads.

mcq.prompt: Why does adding a std::string member change how a by-value struct parameter is passed?
choices: Because the struct grows beyond 16 bytes
Because non-trivial copy and destruction behaviour forces the argument through an invisible pointer with the language's copy machinery
Because std::string members must be passed by const reference
Because the ABI classifies pointers separately from floating-point fields
mcq.explain: Register passing under this ABI requires the type to have no user-defined copy machinery, independent of size. Once copy construction and destruction are non-trivial, the caller materialises the object and passes its address. Size is the rule of thumb; triviality is the actual gate.

reading.explain: == binds tighter than &, so `wrong` is `flags & (snapshot == 0)` — that is `flags & 0`, always zero, always false. The parenthesised version asks the intended question and is true because flags is 0.

Unqualified lookup stops at the innermost scope containing the name, so the local wins. The two qualified spellings reach past it: market::feed::timeout names the namespace member, and ::timeout names the global.
short to int is a promotion, which ranks above the integral conversion to long and the floating conversion to double. Rank decides, not apparent closeness of width.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: unsigned int to int, to long, and to double are all plain conversions of the same rank. No candidate is better than the others for the sole argument, so the call is ambiguous.

The default argument expression is evaluated at each call, not once at the declaration. So the counter advances every time the argument is omitted — a cost and a side effect that are invisible at the call site.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: Deduced return types must agree exactly across every non-discarded return statement. The first return fixes the type as int; the second deduces double and the definitions conflict. Unlike the conditional operator, deduction does not look for a common arithmetic type.

The hidden friend is invisible to ordinary namespace lookup, but ADL adds trading to the candidate search because an argument is a trading::Order. The friend also gets access to the private members it prints.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: Reading one past the end of the array is undefined behaviour — no bounds check exists and nothing is thrown. It usually appears to print whatever adjacent stack bytes hold; ASan reports a stack-buffer-overflow.

writing.prompt: Write four functions over a small `Order { std::int64_t id; double price; }`: read the price from a copy, observe it without permitting modification, modify the price through the caller's object, and return the mid of two doubles using the trailing-return spelling.
checklist: By-value parameter for the copy version
const Order& for the read-only observer
Order& (non-const) for the mutator
Trailing return type spelled `auto mid(...) -> double`
Nothing returns a reference or pointer to a local
writing.notes: The declaration itself is the documentation: a caller reading `reprice(Order&, double)` knows its object may change, and one reading `observe_price(const Order&)` knows it will not.

writing.prompt: `publish(next_bid(), next_ask());` where both helpers increment a shared counter. Rewrite it so the sequence numbers are deterministic, and add a comment saying what rule forced the change.
checklist: Each side effect is computed in its own statement
The statements run in a defined order before the call
Comment names unspecified argument evaluation order
The call itself now takes plain values
writing.notes: Note the precise claim: this is unspecified, not undefined. C++17 guarantees the two calls do not interleave — it just refuses to say which goes first.

writing.prompt: Define a struct Quote in namespace trading with a namespace-scope swap for it, then write a free function that swaps two Quotes using the two-step ADL idiom so a type-specific swap is preferred and std::swap is the fallback.
checklist: trading::swap takes two non-const lvalue references
The caller writes `using std::swap;` inside the function body
The call to swap is unqualified
A comment explains that std::swap(a, b) would suppress ADL
trading::swap is found by ADL, not by a using-directive
writing.notes: Writing std::swap(left, right) directly would compile and work, but it would silently bypass any type-specific swap — the exact opposite of what a generic algorithm wants.

writing.prompt: Given `double mid(double, double)`, declare a pointer to it two ways: directly, and through a type alias. Then call it through the pointer.
checklist: Direct declaration spells `double (*name)(double, double)`
Alias declared with `using` (not a raw typedef of the wrong shape)
Both are initialised from the function name, relying on function-to-pointer decay
The call goes through the pointer
writing.notes: The function name decays to a pointer in the initialiser exactly as an array name decays — `&mid` is equivalent and more explicit. The alias is what makes these storable in containers without unreadable declarations.

writing.prompt: For a struct Order with a `double price` member and a `double notional() const` member function, declare a pointer to the data member and a pointer to the member function, then call each — both directly and through std::invoke.
checklist: Data-member pointer declared as `double Order::*`
Member-function pointer declared as `double (Order::*)() const` — const included
Direct member-function call parenthesised: (order.*pmf)()
std::invoke(pm, order) and std::invoke(pmf, order) for the same operations
Includes <functional>
writing.notes: Dropping the const from the member-function pointer type is the usual mistake — it is part of the type, so `double (Order::*)()` will not bind to a const member function.

writing.prompt: Write a `send_order` returning a bool success flag that the compiler will warn about if a caller ignores it. Add a second function that deliberately discards the result without a warning, and a parameter the function does not use.
checklist: [[nodiscard]] on the returning function
A deliberate discard uses a cast to void (or otherwise consumes the result)
[[maybe_unused]] on the intentionally unused parameter
Attributes are placed on the declaration, before the return type
writing.notes: [[nodiscard]] belongs on results whose omission is probably a bug — error codes above all. Chapter 6 applies it to error values callers must inspect.

writing.prompt: Write the signatures you would use for four argument kinds: an int tick count, a two-double trivial Order, a large read-only object with a std::string member, and a caller-owned object to be modified. One line of comment each, justifying the choice.
checklist: Scalar passed by value
Small trivially copyable aggregate passed by value
Large or non-trivial read-only object passed by const T&
Object to be modified passed by T&
Comments justify by copy cost / register eligibility, not by taste
writing.notes: The 16-byte threshold is SysV x86-64 specific and is a rule of thumb, not a law — the real gate is that the type has no user-defined copy machinery. Measure at the boundaries that matter.

writing.prompt: Write five initialisations that demonstrate reference binding: a non-const lvalue reference to a variable, a const reference to a prvalue, a const reference to a function returning by value, an lvalue reference to a function returning T&, and a commented-out line showing the binding that is rejected.
checklist: int& binds only to a named variable (an lvalue)
const int& binds to an arithmetic prvalue
The commented-out int& binding to a prvalue names why it is rejected
A function returning T& yields an lvalue expression
A function returning T yields a prvalue expression
writing.notes: Classify the expression, not the declaration. `find_value()` is an lvalue expression because the *return type* is a reference; `make_value()` is a prvalue because it returns an object by value.
